## Phelps apologizes after bong photo; experts say image repair may determine endorsement fallout

**AMERICAN MORNING —** Olympic swimmer Michael Phelps, one of the most decorated athletes in history, is facing a public-relations test after a British newspaper published a photograph that appeared to show him smoking from a bong at a party.

The image, published by the *News of the World*, quickly spread online and prompted a statement from Phelps, who apologized for what he called “regrettable” behavior and “bad judgment.” Phelps did not dispute the authenticity of the photo.

The controversy comes just months after Phelps dominated the 2008 Beijing Olympics, winning a record eight gold medals and becoming one of the most marketable athletes in the world.

### Phelps: “This will not happen again”

In his statement, Phelps said he acted in a way that was inconsistent with the image he has worked to build.

“I engaged in behavior which was regrettable and demonstrated bad judgment,” Phelps said. “I’m sorry. I promise my fans and the public it will not happen again.”

The question now is whether sponsors will accept that apology — or decide the incident damages the family-friendly image that helped make Phelps a marketing powerhouse.

### Interview: Sports attorney Ryan Smith on endorsements and image rehabilitation

**KIRAN CHETRY, ANCHOR:**  
Joining us now is sports attorney Ryan Smith. Ryan, thanks for being with us.

**RYAN SMITH, SPORTS ATTORNEY:**  
Thanks for having me.

**CHETRY:**  
Michael Phelps is not just an athlete. He’s a brand. When a photo like this comes out, what are sponsors looking at first?

**SMITH:**  
They’re looking at two things: the contract language and the public reaction. Most endorsement deals have what’s called a morals clause. That gives a company the ability to suspend or terminate a relationship if the athlete does something that brings embarrassment or negative attention to the brand.

**CHETRY:**  
So does this automatically mean sponsors walk away?

**SMITH:**  
Not automatically. It depends on how the company views the seriousness of the conduct, whether it was isolated, and whether consumers are truly outraged or willing to move on. Phelps’ apology matters because it was quick, direct and did not try to blame anyone else. That helps.

**CHETRY:**  
He’s coming off one of the greatest Olympic performances ever. Does that give him more protection?

**SMITH:**  
Absolutely. His value is enormous. Sponsors have invested in him because of his success, work ethic and appeal to young athletes and families. But that also makes the risk bigger. When your brand is built on discipline and inspiration, anything suggesting reckless behavior can be damaging.

**CHETRY:**  
What should Phelps do now if he wants to repair the image?

**SMITH:**  
First, he has to disappear from controversy. No more parties in the headlines. Second, he needs to show accountability — maybe speaking to young athletes about decision-making. Third, he has to get back in the pool and remind people why they admired him in the first place. Winning and staying out of trouble are the best rehabilitation tools.

**CHETRY:**  
Could sponsors demand changes even if they don’t drop him?

**SMITH:**  
Yes. They might pause campaigns, renegotiate terms, or require appearances focused on community service or youth programs. A company may say, “We’re not ending the relationship, but we need you to help restore trust.”

**CHETRY:**  
Is there a difference between legal trouble and image trouble here?

**SMITH:**  
There is. Even if there is no criminal case or no charges, endorsement deals are about reputation. A sponsor doesn’t need a conviction to decide the athlete no longer fits its message. The court of public opinion can matter more than a courtroom.

**CHETRY:**  
Bottom line — can Michael Phelps recover from this?

**SMITH:**  
Yes, he can. But the next few weeks are critical. If this remains a single mistake followed by sincere accountability, people may forgive him. If more stories come out or the apology looks like damage control, sponsors may decide the risk is too high.

### A major test for a post-Olympic superstar

Phelps’ representatives are expected to continue conversations with sponsors as the story develops. While some fans have expressed disappointment, others have pointed to his age and the intense scrutiny placed on Olympic athletes outside competition.

For Phelps, the challenge is now bigger than a race: protecting a public image built over years of record-breaking performances.

As Smith put it, the path forward is clear — accountability, discipline and time.

“America loves redemption stories,” Smith said. “But the athlete has to do the work to earn that second chance.”

## Q&A: Sports attorney Ryan Smith on possible consequences

**CNN:** Does the photo alone amount to an anti-doping violation?

**Ryan Smith:** Not necessarily. Anti-doping cases usually require evidence such as a positive drug test, possession, trafficking, or an admission tied to a prohibited substance under the applicable rules. A photograph can create suspicion, but by itself it may not be enough to prove a violation.

**CNN:** How would the World Anti-Doping Agency, or WADA, look at marijuana?

**Smith:** WADA has rules on cannabinoids, but the timing matters. Marijuana is generally treated as prohibited **in competition**, not necessarily at all times. So if an athlete tested positive during an in-competition period, that could trigger sanctions. But if alleged use occurred out of competition and there is no failed test, it becomes much more complicated.

**CNN:** So if Phelps did not fail a drug test, WADA may not have a case?

**Smith:** Correct. Without a positive test or stronger evidence of a rule violation, WADA itself would be limited. Sports federations and national governing bodies may still review the conduct under their own codes of behavior, but that is separate from a classic doping violation.

**CNN:** Could USA Swimming or the U.S. Olympic Committee discipline him anyway?

**Smith:** Yes. Governing bodies often have conduct policies requiring athletes to act in a way that reflects well on the sport. Even if there is no anti-doping penalty, an athlete can face suspension, loss of support, or other discipline for conduct deemed inappropriate.

**CNN:** What about criminal exposure?

**Smith:** That would depend on jurisdiction, evidence, and whether law enforcement had any interest in pursuing it. A published photo alone does not automatically mean charges will follow. Prosecutors would need admissible evidence and a basis to prove an offense.

**CNN:** The bigger impact may be endorsements. How vulnerable is Phelps there?

**Smith:** Very vulnerable. Endorsement contracts usually contain morality clauses. Those clauses allow companies to suspend or terminate deals if an athlete’s conduct damages the brand or brings negative publicity. Even when there is no legal finding, sponsors can decide the association is no longer worth the risk.

**CNN:** Is an apology enough to protect those deals?

**Smith:** Sometimes. It depends on the athlete’s reputation, the sponsor’s audience, and how quickly the controversy fades. Phelps has enormous goodwill because of his Olympic success, but sponsors are highly sensitive to drug-related headlines, especially when an athlete is marketed to families and young fans.

**CNN:** What is the likely outcome?

**Smith:** The most likely outcome is reputational damage, possible discipline from swimming authorities, and sponsor-by-sponsor decisions. Unless there is a positive drug test or additional evidence, this is more likely to be handled as a conduct and public-image matter than a major anti-doping case.

---

Phelps’ apology appears aimed at limiting the fallout before it affects his competitive future or commercial partnerships. But for an athlete whose image has been built on discipline, sacrifice, and Olympic excellence, the photograph has created the first major controversy of his post-Beijing career.

**Sponsor questions swirl after Michael Phelps marijuana photo**

*By [Your Name]*

Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian in history and one of the most marketable athletes in the world, is facing a different kind of race: containing the fallout from a photograph that appeared to show him using a marijuana pipe at a party.

The image, published by a British tabloid, has prompted questions about whether major sponsors will stand by the Olympic swimmer or cut ties to protect their brands. Phelps has apologized publicly, calling his behavior “regrettable” and acknowledging that he used “bad judgment.”

For companies that built campaigns around Phelps’ discipline, focus and clean-cut appeal, the episode presents a familiar dilemma: Is the incident a temporary lapse by a young celebrity, or a breach of the values that made him so valuable in the first place?

### Sponsors weigh image against investment

Phelps’ endorsement portfolio has included major consumer brands, athletic companies and lifestyle products seeking to associate themselves with his record-breaking success. After his dominant Olympic performances, he became more than an athlete; he became a symbol of preparation, sacrifice and achievement.

That brand image is exactly why the marijuana photo could concern sponsors.

Companies typically include “morals clauses” in endorsement contracts, allowing them to suspend or terminate deals if an athlete engages in conduct that brings public disrepute, embarrassment or negative attention to the brand. Whether a sponsor invokes that clause depends on several factors: the wording of the contract, the severity of the conduct, public reaction and the company’s tolerance for controversy.

A sponsor aimed at families or youth consumers may face more pressure to respond aggressively. A brand with a younger or more forgiving customer base may prefer to wait out the news cycle.

In many cases, experts say, sponsors do not immediately drop a top-tier athlete unless the conduct is criminally charged, repeated or directly conflicts with the company’s core identity.

### Legal risks may be limited, but not irrelevant

A sports attorney advising Phelps would likely begin with damage control.

The first step, the attorney would say, is to review every endorsement contract for morals clauses, disclosure requirements and termination provisions. Some agreements may require the athlete to notify sponsors promptly of any controversy. Others may give sponsors broad discretion to act if they believe the athlete has damaged the brand.

The lawyer would also examine whether there is any realistic criminal exposure. A photograph alone may not always be enough to support charges, particularly if authorities cannot establish key details such as the date, location, substance involved or chain of custody. Still, the attorney would advise against making detailed public statements that could create unnecessary legal risk.

The safest legal posture: apologize, take responsibility in general terms and avoid providing specifics that could be used in an investigation or contract dispute.

### Public relations strategy: act quickly, sound sincere

From a public relations standpoint, the advice would be direct: move fast, be accountable and do not appear defensive.

A sports attorney working with a crisis communications team would likely recommend that Phelps:

- Issue a prompt apology acknowledging poor judgment.
- Reaffirm his commitment to fans, teammates and sponsors.
- Avoid blaming the media or the people who took the photo.
- Contact major sponsors privately before they are forced to respond publicly.
- Consider community service or youth-focused outreach if appropriate.
- Stay out of public party settings while the controversy is active.

The goal would be to frame the incident as a mistake rather than a pattern.

For an athlete with Phelps’ record, public goodwill matters. Fans may be disappointed, but many may also be willing to forgive if they believe the apology is genuine and the behavior is isolated.

### Sponsors may prefer a pause over a breakup

For sponsors, the decision is not only moral but commercial. Dropping Phelps could protect a brand from criticism, but it could also mean walking away from one of the most recognizable athletes in the world.

Companies may choose intermediate steps: issuing statements of disappointment, suspending appearances, delaying advertisements or privately warning the athlete that future incidents will end the relationship.

That approach allows sponsors to show concern without making a permanent decision during the peak of the controversy.

If the news cycle fades and Phelps avoids further trouble, many brands may decide the long-term value of the relationship outweighs the short-term embarrassment.

### Reputation remains the central issue

The scandal is unlikely to erase Phelps’ Olympic legacy, but it could complicate the business empire built around it. Endorsement deals depend on trust, and sponsors pay elite athletes not only for medals but for meaning.

A sports attorney’s message to Phelps would be simple: protect the contracts, protect the reputation and avoid turning one bad photograph into a larger crisis.

Whether sponsors stay or go may depend less on the image itself than on what Phelps does next.
